title: Incremental deferred tool invocation and SDK hydration notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a pragmatic approach for supporting deferred (lazy) tool invocation inside hosted streaming responses while keeping SDK ergonomics simple for integrators. Aim: minimize blocking latency for clients, allow partial/structured outputs early, and provide safe, resumable hydration of tool outputs (stubs -> full results).

Problem statement / user stories:
- User wants to stream partial reasoning and let the client show intermediate answers (progressive UI) while some external tool calls (API lookups, DB queries) are expensive and should not block the whole response.
- Integrator wants predictable contracts: when a tool is invoked, the SDK should expose a stable stub that can be hydrated later without rewriting app logic.
- Mobile/offline clients need a compact representation (stubs) to show immediate affordances and avoid large payloads.

Key concepts proposed:
1) Deferred Tool Invocation: model can emit a special token frame representing a tool request (tool-stub) rather than awaiting tool completion. The server returns the stub immediately in the stream; the runtime enqueues the real invocation.
2) Hydration Lifecycle: stubs carry an id + minimal schema (type, confidence, ETA estimate, fallback text). Clients/SDKs can subscribe to hydration updates or poll a hydration endpoint to receive replacement frames.
3) Progressive Frames: introduce typed delta frames: 'partial-text', 'tool-stub', 'tool-hydration', 'tool-fallback', 'finalize'. Each frame is small and parseable; client can merge into existing transcript.
4) Adaptive Batching & Backoff: backend groups deferred tool invocations across requests to amortize call overhead; if a tool system reports high latency, server can switch stubs to optimistic/fallback text automatically.
5) SDK ergonomics: provide 3-level API: (a) streaming iterator that yields frames, (b) high-level convenience wrapper that maps stubs to Promises/async await hydration handles, (c) low-bandwidth mobile binding that emits compact stub-only events.

Protocol sketch:
- Stream line: text frames are yielded as usual. When model emits a tool-stub frame, it contains: stub_id, tool_name, minimal_payload_hash, schema_hint, expected_update_ttl.
- Server ACKs the stub and returns an initial hydration state: queued | executing | failed | done (with replaceable payload).
- Hydration push: server may push 'tool-hydration' frames to the original stream when result arrives, optionally as a replace instruction (replace frame id X with payload Y). If replacement cannot be streamed (client disconnected), result stored under hydration endpoint /sessions/{sid}/stubs/{stub_id}.

Client/SDK behavior patterns:
- Default: SDK exposes stream frames; app-level developer can ignore tool stubs and just show partial text.
- Promise wrapper: SDK returns a hydration promise per stub which resolves when final result arrives; if unresolved by timeout, the Promise rejects or yields fallback depending on config.
- Optimistic-ui mode: SDK can locally render a best-effort summary derived from schema_hint when server-side hydration is slow.

Operational & observability needs:
- Telemetry: stub lifecycle events (queued, executed, retry, fail, done), latency histograms per tool_name, correlation ids to link stream session -> backend invocation.
- Cost accounting: deferred invocations should be tracked and presented separately from token usage.
- Rollout controls: feature flag to enable deferred tool invocation per-customer / per-model.

Open design questions / tradeoffs:
- Consistency model: replacement semantics (opaque replace vs. merge diffs). Replace is simpler but loses incremental edits. Merge diffs are complex and error-prone for structured outputs.
- Security/Privacy: storing hydrated tool outputs in session endpoints raises retention/KMS needs; propose default TTL of 24h and tenant-level overrides.
- Failure handling UX: should SDK auto-fallback to a canned response or surface error for app to handle? Recommend configurable fallback policy with safe defaults (non-actionable fallback text).
- Backpressure: how to surface queuing delays to client without spamming the UI? Suggest status updates with exponential backoff.

Implementation roadmap (MVP -> M1 -> M2):
- MVP (6w): streaming stub frames + server-side queued invocations + hydration endpoint; minimal streaming push when connected; simple SDK Promise wrapper.
- M1 (8w after MVP): batching backend, observability dashboards, mobile compact binding, fallback policies, per-tenant feature flags.
- M2 (Q3): schema-first replace/merge semantics, SDK helpers for structured result reconciliation, offline-first sync and resumable hydration across devices.

Compatibility notes with existing hosted API patterns:
- Reuse existing streaming transport (current chunk frames) but add a typed header to each frame. Backwards compatibility: older SDKs will render stub frames as text fallback; recommend server also send a short textual placeholder in legacy text_chunk.

Acceptance criteria (for go/no-go):
- Streaming sessions can emit stubs and receive hydration pushes in <90th percentile latency of 2s for cached tools and <3s for batched external integrations in controlled tests.
- SDK Promise wrapper covers 90% of internal sample apps with <=5 lines of glue code.
- Observability: tenant dashboard shows average stub hydration time and error rate.

Notes to reviewers / next steps:
- Collect list of top 10 external tool integrations and their failure modes (Devon to reach out to Solutions Eng).
- Spike: small bench to measure batching gains for common tool patterns (Hannah).
- UX mockups for stub placeholders vs. final hydrate states (Miguel).

This doc intentionally leaves protocol fields underspecified; goal is to capture the product intent and SDK ergonomics for alignment with runtime/serving and SDK owners.

Unresolved: should stubs be addressable across sessions (global stub id) to allow deduping? pros: fewer duplicate invocations; cons: caching complexity and privacy.

Discussion thread: #hosted-api-protocol on Slack.
